traces.answer:
So we had a bunch of interesting news in venture this week:
Canva raised another huge round at a stunning $65 Billion (!)
Atlassian co-founders were forced out by the board,
And Stripe announced no more late-stage VC rounds
.
But there’s also something even bigger going on here:  The Age of Acqui-Hire Is Back.  And This Time It’s Even Louder.
The latest example is Capital One buying Brex for $5.15 billion — which represents a roughly 57% premium to their last private market valuation of $12.3 Billion in October 2022 (see [E1]). But how much of that will go towards “buying” Brex itself?
Brexpense was one of Brex’s core products. It didn’t work well, and they shut it down. So what exactly does Capital One get here? A lot … of nothing.
This isn’t entirely new though.  We’ve seen many other similar deals over the past few months:
ServiceTitan bought $1B+ ARR competitor Workwave for $1B cash + stock, paying almost twice as much as the last round ($600m) — but likely getting very little real business back.  ServiceTitan already has a strong presence in plumbing, HVAC, etc. and Workwave is primarily electrical contracting.  How much overlap really is there here? Not much.
Thoma Bravo bought SaaS leader Qualtrics for ~$13B, then spun it off again a year later. Why? They got a ton of cash in the deal. Not sure Thoma Bravo made any money here, per se.  But I’m pretty sure they did make a ton of cash doing the deal.  Cash always makes money.
Veeva bought Vanta, a security startup, for a reported $3.35 billion. Security startups rarely command such high valuations.
Samsara paid $800M to acquire Fleetmatics’ UK operations, and then shut them down
Salesforce spent $27 billion on Slack
Monday.com sold Salesloft for $2.85 billion
HubSpot
bought Customer.io
for $45 million.

retrieval_hits.text:
Capital One just announced it’s acquiring Brex for $5.15 billion.  An incredible, top 0.1% “exit” in less than 10 years from a category creator that created massive wealth and opportunities.  A huge win.
But also … less than half of Brex’s $12.3 billion valuation from October 2022.
Should anyone care?  Many are seeing is a failure vs Ramp, a measured success at best.  But … why?
I don’t think most people commenting on this actually understand what they’re reacting to. What they’re really feeling—even if they can’t articulate it—is the consequences of
hubristic fundraising
.
And we should probably talk about it. Because hubristic fundraising is back. In a big way. It was back big time in 2025 and is back even bigger time in 2026.
First, What Is Hubristic Fundraising?
Let me define it simply: Hubristic fundraising is when you raise at a valuation so aggressive, with terms so favorable, with a narrative so bold, that you are essentially betting the entire future of your company on hitting an extraordinary outcome.
It’s not just “raising a lot of money.” Plenty of companies raise hundreds of millions without hubris.
Hubristic fundraising is when you:
Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple.  Often, again and again.
Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”
Create expectations that anything less than a $20B+ IPO or massive strategic exit is a disappointment
These deals can work out.  It will work out for Databricks, Anthropic, etc.  But at least as of when I write this, there are so very few $30B+

building sustainable competitive moats. Revenue Velocity
Canva, which is now valued at $40 billion, added $157 million in value daily since its prior funding in April 2021. These aren’t incremental growth stories—they’re companies experiencing parabolic expansion in massive markets. Market Timing and Category Creation
The current decacorn landscape is dominated by companies that didn’t just enter existing markets—they created entirely new categories.

From fintech startups like Stripe and Revolut to AI leaders like OpenAI, these companies represent the pinnacle of startup success. The New Exit Math
The traditional venture capital power law is becoming even more extreme. Stanford’s data confirms this concentration: only 33 companies have achieved decacorn exits, representing just 6% of all unicorn exits but likely driving a disproportionate share of venture returns. The reality check for VCs:
Only 6% of unicorn exits achieve decacorn status ($10B+)
88% of decacorn exits happen through IPOs, not acquisitions
55% of unicorns exit in the narrow $1-2B range, suggesting limited value creation beyond initial unicorn status
40% of US unicorns have been held in portfolios for at least nine years, and that group accounts for more than $1 trillion in value
Will AI Change the Math? (That’s The Bet We’re All Making, At Least)
The emergence of artificial intelligence as a dominant force in venture capital is fundamentally altering the unicorn-to-decacorn trajectory in ways that Stanford’s historical data couldn’t have predicted. Early 2025 marked the highest VC investment in AI on record, with global AI-related deals totaling $73.1 billion, accounting for 57.9% of all VC-backed funding. This isn’t just a trend—it’s a seismic shift that may rewrite the rules of startup valuations. The AI Unicorn Speed Run

Let me define it simply: Hubristic fundraising is when you raise at a valuation so aggressive, with terms so favorable, with a narrative so bold, that you are essentially betting the entire future of your company on hitting an extraordinary outcome.

Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple.  Often, again and again.
Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”
Create expectations that anything less than a $20B+ IPO or massive strategic exit is a disappointment

traces.answer: So we've talked a lot over the years about how valuations in venture go up, down, everywhere and all around -- and I think there has never been as much hubris in venture capital as today. And one way to see this is looking back at who bought whom, especially where they paid what. This is something everyone knows how to do. But my point here is let's look at what happened recently because it tells us a lot about the state of things right now. So Brex had raised at a $12.3 billion valuation last year. It's a great product, a great team, but really a niche player in business expense cards. Now, many folks will say well, why would anyone buy a startup at $12 billion unless they're going to IPO? You need to triple that. If you can get to a $30 billion valuation after five or six years, then you could return 300% plus on your money if you invest at 12. But most startups don't make that journey. They don't even come close. That means you got to be very careful investing at high prices. Because ultimately, almost no matter what happens, that valuation needs to be tripled, quadrupled, or more to truly deliver the returns investors want. And also importantly, you'll hear a lot about "hubristic" fundraising these days. My definition of hubristic fundraising is when you fundraise at such a high valuation that you're literally betting everything on having to hit a top decile outcome. In essence, raising at 50x to 200x times revenue multiples. The problem is this creates unrealistic expectations for both founders and VCs alike.

traces.answer:
So we’ve done so many SaaStr Annuals now (11!), and talked with so many VPs of Sales.  And I’m fairly confident this is the first time someone asked me directly if hiring enough VPs of Sales was my top advice for how to scale past $10m-$20m ARR.  It wasn’t.  My #1 advice at that stage for scaling sales is:
Hire a Great VP of Sales, even if you don’t have all their quotas hit yet
.
More on that here:
The Best VP of Sales Hires Even More Great Sales Executives — Immediately | SaaStr
But … there are caveats.  In fact, 7 of them per the above tweet:
Don’t hire a Stretch VP of Sales Who Has Never Hired Quota-Hitters Before
.
This just doesn’t work out well.  You need someone that knows how to recruit and close quota-hitters fast.  If your VP of Sales can’t get you her own team to success by month 3-4 max, she’s failed.  No one wants to join a losing ship.  Hire a real one instead. Don’t hire a VP of Sales From Another Hot Startup Where Everyone Makes Ton$$.   They will want everyone to make tons of money as well. They’ll expect almost everyone to be making big bonuses. They won’t really understand selling to SMBs, or even medium-sized customers, unless they came up through that. They’ll spend way too much time managing individual relationships. And usually, no matter what they tell you, they haven’t actually been a true individual contributor since $15m+ ARR.  A related post
here
. Don’t Hire Someone To Be Your VP of Sales That Doesn’t Want to Do All The Interviews Themselves
. This always ends badly. Don’t Let Them Stay When Things Aren’t Working Out.  Get On Plan By Month 3.

Hire a Great VP of Sales, even if you don’t have all their quotas hit yet
.
More on that here:
The Best VP of Sales Hires Even More Great Sales Executives — Immediately | SaaStr
But … there are caveats.  In fact, 7 of them per the above tweet:
Don’t hire a Stretch VP of Sales Who Has Never Hired Quota-Hitters Before
.
This just doesn’t work out well.  You need someone that knows how to recruit and close quota-hitters fast.  If your VP of Sales can’t get you her own team to success by month 3-4 max, she’s failed.  No one wants to join a losing ship.  Hire a real one instead. Don’t hire a VP of Sales From Another Hot Startup Where Everyone Makes Ton$$.   They will want everyone to make tons of money as well. They’ll expect almost everyone to be making big bonuses. They won’t really understand selling to SMBs, or even medium-sized customers, unless they came up through that. They’ll spend way too much time managing individual relationships. And usually, no matter what they tell you, they haven’t actually been a true individual contributor since $15m+ ARR.  A related post

They’re not bad. They’re not great. They’re just… fine.

They hit their numbers, manage their team adequately, and never cause drama. But they also never drive breakthrough results or inspire their organization. In a growth company, “fine” is actually terrible. The Kindness Trap

We all get it. We’ve all been there. The VP who worked 80-hour weeks in the early days. The one who took a pay cut to join your mission. The one whose family you know, whose kids you know. traces.answer:
So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about hiring a great VP of Sales. How to hire one. What mistakes you make when you don't hire a good one. But there are two issues that sort of pop up all the time. And so let me just address them today because they're really important. The first one is this question of whether or not you can criticize your VP of Sales if she's not performing well. This comes up a lot with founders. It always does. So many times as an investor, I see folks just take criticism poorly when their VPs aren't doing well. They start off being very constructive. "Hey, we need to increase our pipeline here." Then later, "We haven't closed enough deals," and then finally, "This is your fault."
And what happens after that is often, the team disbands. It breaks apart. Because no one likes to be yelled at, especially by someone they work for, right?
E1
. When things get tough, everyone gets criticized. If a VP of Sales isn't meeting her number, and even worse, her boss starts taking shots at her, it doesn't help anything. In fact, my advice almost universally is to keep any VP-level exec that didn't perform well, any that wasn't truly great, is keep them until you find a replacement. Even if they failed, even if they weren't good enough. My top piece of advice is keep them. You will probably fail again without them. Your VP of Engineering can ship code faster with him than without him. Maybe your VP of Product was great at product management and strategy. Keep her until you have another idea. Don't go out and hire some hot new VP of Product who hasn't worked anywhere like yours. Same thing with marketing and everything else. These roles have different phases. They have different life cycles. There's discovery. There's building something out. There's scaling. And if you fire these guys during different parts of the cycle, you'll mess things up.

"AI means eveything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience. A workflow that surfaces the job that needs to get done -- and just does it. That's the Future of Enterprise SaaS" Rubrik CPO Anneka Gupta New -> "Going Multi-Product in the Age of AI with CPOs of Webflow, Rubrik, Zoom, and Productboard" https://lnkd.in/gQFeDYeT

The SaaS Era of 2013-2022 is Over. Welcome to The World of Hyperfunctional SaaS. So is AI taking over everything? Will $1B SaaS companies be run by 1 person teams? I mean … maybe. Across the SaaStr Fund portfolio, I’ve seen multiple portfolio companies lose $1m customers to new, in-house AI initiatives. But I’ve also seen others grow even faster as AI rebooted and enhanced their products. What I do know is many of the billion+ SaaS companies I invested in a decade ago would not be remotely competitive today. And that’s how it should be. Software, innovation and time marches on. And if you can’t keep up, you’ll get left behind. Many today have been unable to keep up, and have fallen behind, and seen growth slow to 20%, 10%, even 0%. What I really think is happening is customer expectations have gone way up. AI is part of it, platforms are part of it. And promises are part of it. We’re promising to do a lot more. Today, customers are expecting: 1⃣ AI to replace 30%-50% of their workforce. Is this possible? Maybe, maybe not. But it’s already starting in the contact center, where leaders from @Zendesk to @gorgiasio to @intercom to @Talkdesk are automating away 30%-50% of contact center headcount. 2⃣ All unstructured data to be instantly structured and searchable. Search was sleepy for years. Now, it’s front and center. Products that were complex to extract data before, especially documents, can now be organized in real-time by AI. This is one reason @levie is so excited about AI. It unlocks all your documents. Customers aren’t satisfied anymore with not being able to get answers from every and any dataset. 3⃣ Every product to work elegantly in a plain English prompt. We

Human-in-the-loop and AI orchestration are the most misunderstood concepts in B2B SaaS. 1️⃣ Most think "human-in-the-loop" means AI makes their work easier. Wrong. 👋 It means humans handle the cases AI can't solve. All day long. In real time, or as close as possible. The 30% of support tickets that are too complex. The sales conversations that need real judgment. The edge cases that break automated systems. 🚵 As AI gets better, the remaining human work gets HARDER, not easier. 2️⃣ And "orchestration" isn't picking vendors and watching dashboards. It's 60+ days of intensive training after deployment. Daily quality auditing. Managing 5-10 AI systems that each have unique failure modes. 👉 SaaStr's reality check: We sent 4,495 AI emails with top response rates, but it required: • 90 minutes every morning training the AI • 1 hour every night reviewing performance • Real-time responses throughout the day • 20+ million words of training content 🫵 Doing AI right is more work than not using AI at all Perplexity's CBO revealed another layer at SaaStr AI Summit 2025: AI changes WHEN you work, not just what you do. Sales reps now use AI live during prospect calls, making split-second decisions about what intelligence to surface while maintaining authentic conversations. Support already proved this model works: • Decagon: 70% deflection rates • Duolingo: 80%+ automation • Intercom: 86% resolution rates But those numbers hide the human orchestration behind them. Support teams evolved into AI managers, not disappearing but becoming more specialized. They do the tough stuff now. The multiplication effect hits when you deploy >multiple< AI systems. Now you need people who understand how your chatbot's limitations interact with your email automation's strengths. How to prevent AI systems from amplifying each other's errors. The uncomfortable truth: AI

from these three companies extend far beyond AI:
Question Annual Planning
: In rapidly evolving markets, shorter planning cycles may be more effective than traditional annual quotas and targets. Hire Technical Sales Talent
: As products become more sophisticated, sales teams need deeper technical understanding to be effective. Embrace Product-Led Growth
: When possible, focus on fulfilling demand rather than generating it through traditional sales and marketing motions. Use Your Own Product
: Internal usage creates better products and more authentic customer conversations. Collaborate with Competitors
: In emerging markets, ecosystem advancement can benefit all players. The traditional SaaS sales playbook assumed predictable growth, high gross margins, and demand generation challenges. AI companies operate in a world of unpredictable hypergrowth, real marginal costs, and demand fulfillment opportunities. The companies that recognize this shift earliest—and adapt their go-to-market strategies accordingly—will define the next era of enterprise software.

Quotable Moments
Gorkem Yurtseven (FAL)
:
“We thought doubling next year would be a good target for quotas. During the interviews, we grew maybe 50%. We were almost halfway there already. We decided this is useless. We are not doing quotas.”
Kelly Loftus (Anthropic)
:
“We still don’t really have quotas. We have shadow targets. It’s really hard to predict exactly what is happening when adoption is fast and driven by model intelligence you cannot predict over a long time period.”
Jacob Jackson (Cursor)
:
“Many of our first enterprise customers bought Cursor because their developers came to management and said we need this tool—or in many cases they were already using it.”
Talia Goldberg (Bessemer)
:
“COGs are the new CAC. You can spend a lot on cost of goods sold, but you can’t be spending a lot on customer acquisition when you have low margins and high acquisition costs.”

The SaaS Era of 2013-2022 is Over. Welcome to The World of Hyperfunctional SaaS. So is AI taking over everything? Will $1B SaaS companies be run by 1 person teams? I mean … maybe. Across the SaaStr Fund portfolio, I’ve seen multiple portfolio companies lose $1m customers to new, in-house AI initiatives. But I’ve also seen others grow even faster as AI rebooted and enhanced their products. What I do know is many of the billion+ SaaS companies I invested in a decade ago would not be remotely competitive today. And that’s how it should be. Software, innovation and time marches on. And if you can’t keep up, you’ll get left behind. Many today have been unable to keep up, and have fallen behind, and seen growth slow to 20%, 10%, even 0%. What I really think is happening is customer expectations have gone way up. AI is part of it, platforms are part of it. And promises are part of it. We’re promising to do a lot more. Today, customers are expecting: 1⃣ AI to replace 30%-50% of their workforce. Is this possible? Maybe, maybe not. But it’s already starting in the contact center, where leaders from @Zendesk to @gorgiasio to @intercom to @Talkdesk are automating away 30%-50% of contact center headcount. 2⃣ All unstructured data to be instantly structured and searchable. Search was sleepy for years. Now, it’s front and center. Products that were complex to extract data before, especially documents, can now be organized in real-time by AI. This is one reason @levie is so excited about AI. It unlocks all your documents. Customers aren’t satisfied anymore with not being able to get answers from every and any dataset. 3⃣ Every product to work elegantly in a plain English prompt. We

[gd_4f6908ae4b2f4c4e20daccaa]
Attribution status: named_author. Do not treat the passage as Jason Lemkin's personal position unless the passage itself says so.
Human-in-the-loop and AI orchestration are the most misunderstood concepts in B2B SaaS. 1️⃣ Most think "human-in-the-loop" means AI makes their work easier. Wrong. 👋 It means humans handle the cases AI can't solve. All day long. In real time, or as close as possible. The 30% of support tickets that are too complex. The sales conversations that need real judgment. The edge cases that break automated systems. 🚵 As AI gets better, the remaining human work gets HARDER, not easier. 2️⃣ And "orchestration" isn't picking vendors and watching dashboards. It's 60+ days of intensive training after deployment. Daily quality auditing. Managing 5-10 AI systems that each have unique failure modes. 👉 SaaStr's reality check: We sent 4,495 AI emails with top response rates, but it required: • 90 minutes every morning training the AI • 1 hour every night reviewing performance • Real-time responses throughout the day • 20+ million words of training content 🫵 Doing AI right is more work than not using AI at all Perplexity's CBO revealed another layer at SaaStr AI Summit 2025: AI changes WHEN you work, not just what you do. Sales reps now use AI live during prospect calls, making split-second decisions about what intelligence to surface while maintaining authentic conversations. Support already proved this model works: • Decagon: 70% deflection rates • Duolingo: 80%+ automation • Intercom: 86% resolution rates But those numbers hide the human orchestration behind them. Support teams evolved into AI managers, not disappearing but becoming more specialized. They do the tough stuff now. The multiplication effect hits when you deploy >multiple< AI systems. Now you need people who understand how your chatbot's limitations interact with your email automation's strengths. How to prevent AI systems from amplifying each other's errors. The uncomfortable truth: AI

from these three companies extend far beyond AI:
Question Annual Planning
: In rapidly evolving markets, shorter planning cycles may be more effective than traditional annual quotas and targets. Hire Technical Sales Talent
: As products become more sophisticated, sales teams need deeper technical understanding to be effective. Embrace Product-Led Growth
: When possible, focus on fulfilling demand rather than generating it through traditional sales and marketing motions. Use Your Own Product
: Internal usage creates better products and more authentic customer conversations. Collaborate with Competitors
: In emerging markets, ecosystem advancement can benefit all players. The traditional SaaS sales playbook assumed predictable growth, high gross margins, and demand generation challenges. AI companies operate in a world of unpredictable hypergrowth, real marginal costs, and demand fulfillment opportunities. The companies that recognize this shift earliest—and adapt their go-to-market strategies accordingly—will define the next era of enterprise software.

Quotable Moments
Gorkem Yurtseven (FAL)
:
“We thought doubling next year would be a good target for quotas. During the interviews, we grew maybe 50%. We were almost halfway there already. We decided this is useless. We are not doing quotas.”
Kelly Loftus (Anthropic)
:
“We still don’t really have quotas. We have shadow targets. It’s really hard to predict exactly what is happening when adoption is fast and driven by model intelligence you cannot predict over a long time period.”
Jacob Jackson (Cursor)
:
“Many of our first enterprise customers bought Cursor because their developers came to management and said we need this tool—or in many cases they were already using it.”
Talia Goldberg (Bessemer)
:
“COGs are the new CAC. You can spend a lot on cost of goods sold, but you can’t be spending a lot on customer acquisition when you have low margins and high acquisition costs.”

So as we start off here at SaaStr Annual this week,
we're gonna have over 20 sessions on AI
and many of them will say that's one thing you need to do with your app.
That's one big promise around AI.
That you don't need to sell to every single user anymore.
And maybe some things even more than that.
But what if I told you right now the majority of those apps I've invested in wouldn't be remotely competitive today?
The reality is there's a lot of competition out there and these expectations are coming up fast for us all.
Let me share just one example.
I was talking to the CEO of an amazing startup called Flock Safety.
It's worth billions of dollars already.
They were founded by a great founder who sold his last company for $100 million cash.
He wanted to go back into safety.
His family had been killed in a crime when he was younger.
Flock Safety is a phenomenal platform used by police departments, security guards, event organizers.
People use it to track down people they want to catch.
This guy built it, launched it, got to $25 million ARR, hired a COO, and then stepped aside because he didn't know how to scale past that point.
Fast forward five years later, he came back.
What happened during the five year gap?
There were 200 competitors in the space.
Not 10 or 15, but 200.
The market shrunk.
Many of those startups couldn't raise money, so they died.
Others got acquired, but he still found a way to come back, rebuild the team, get to another IPO candidate, and it's growing faster than ever.
Here's the thing.
AI isn't changing our business models overnight.
We've seen this before.
But it's accelerating change.
It's making everyone nervous.
It's creating new winners and losers.
Even folks like Flock Safety, which is doing well, they're nervous.
Because they see the threat and the opportunity ahead.
It makes sense.
So let's distill down what AI does mean for SaaS today.
Jason M. Lemkin
@jasonlk
 
@rodriscoll
 + 
@HarryStebbings
:

"You can't make the same mistakes twice. That's why I'm not interested in investing in anything I did worse than once."
traces.raw_model_output: So who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience? Well, one thing we all know is that many of the billion-dollar plus SaaS companies I invested in a decade ago would not be remotely competitive today because they were very much built around one size fits all products for an average use case. So there's no question there's been change in how you build software with AI. That being said, it seems like this idea that everyone has to personalize every single piece of software to every user at scale when maybe the reality is that's just not true. There's so much value in having simple interfaces where you have broad functionality that works well for your typical user. You don't need to make everything customizable. Even though some people want to do it. So my point is if you're building enterprise software, you got to think really hard before you try to customize things way too far. Now, one last thing. When I look back on all the investments I've made over the years, I'm surprised by one thing: none of these unicorn and decacorn companies that I invested in even a decade ago would be remotely competitive today. This isn't quite true. Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk, etc. are still super successful, but they aren't as innovative or ahead of the curve as they once were. But what they lack now is innovation. None of them had AI agents, which is why I call them the "old guard". They didn't have AI features per se, but they did innovate in areas related to AI. The next big wave of unicorns are going to take advantage of this. What's cool about the next wave is that the old guard is still out there, so the bar hasn't gone up. If you're able to win customers away from the incumbents, you'll be rewarded.

The SaaS Era of 2013-2022 is Over. Welcome to The World of Hyperfunctional SaaS. So is AI taking over everything? Will $1B SaaS companies be run by 1 person teams? I mean … maybe. Across the SaaStr Fund portfolio, I’ve seen multiple portfolio companies lose $1m customers to new, in-house AI initiatives. But I’ve also seen others grow even faster as AI rebooted and enhanced their products. What I do know is many of the billion+ SaaS companies I invested in a decade ago would not be remotely competitive today. And that’s how it should be. Software, innovation and time marches on. And if you can’t keep up, you’ll get left behind. Many today have been unable to keep up, and have fallen behind, and seen growth slow to 20%, 10%, even 0%. What I really think is happening is customer expectations have gone way up. AI is part of it, platforms are part of it. And promises are part of it. We’re promising to do a lot more. Today, customers are expecting: 1⃣ AI to replace 30%-50% of their workforce. Is this possible? Maybe, maybe not. But it’s already starting in the contact center, where leaders from @Zendesk to @gorgiasio to @intercom to @Talkdesk are automating away 30%-50% of contact center headcount. 2⃣ All unstructured data to be instantly structured and searchable. Search was sleepy for years. Now, it’s front and center. Products that were complex to extract data before, especially documents, can now be organized in real-time by AI. This is one reason @levie is so excited about AI. It unlocks all your documents. Customers aren’t satisfied anymore with not being able to get answers from every and any dataset. 3⃣ Every product to work elegantly in a plain English prompt. We

Human-in-the-loop and AI orchestration are the most misunderstood concepts in B2B SaaS. 1️⃣ Most think "human-in-the-loop" means AI makes their work easier. Wrong. 👋 It means humans handle the cases AI can't solve. All day long. In real time, or as close as possible. The 30% of support tickets that are too complex. The sales conversations that need real judgment. The edge cases that break automated systems. 🚵 As AI gets better, the remaining human work gets HARDER, not easier. 2️⃣ And "orchestration" isn't picking vendors and watching dashboards. It's 60+ days of intensive training after deployment. Daily quality auditing. Managing 5-10 AI systems that each have unique failure modes. 👉 SaaStr's reality check: We sent 4,495 AI emails with top response rates, but it required: • 90 minutes every morning training the AI • 1 hour every night reviewing performance • Real-time responses throughout the day • 20+ million words of training content 🫵 Doing AI right is more work than not using AI at all Perplexity's CBO revealed another layer at SaaStr AI Summit 2025: AI changes WHEN you work, not just what you do. Sales reps now use AI live during prospect calls, making split-second decisions about what intelligence to surface while maintaining authentic conversations. Support already proved this model works: • Decagon: 70% deflection rates • Duolingo: 80%+ automation • Intercom: 86% resolution rates But those numbers hide the human orchestration behind them. Support teams evolved into AI managers, not disappearing but becoming more specialized. They do the tough stuff now. The multiplication effect hits when you deploy >multiple< AI systems. Now you need people who understand how your chatbot's limitations interact with your email automation's strengths. How to prevent AI systems from amplifying each other's errors. The uncomfortable truth: AI

from these three companies extend far beyond AI:
Question Annual Planning
: In rapidly evolving markets, shorter planning cycles may be more effective than traditional annual quotas and targets. Hire Technical Sales Talent
: As products become more sophisticated, sales teams need deeper technical understanding to be effective. Embrace Product-Led Growth
: When possible, focus on fulfilling demand rather than generating it through traditional sales and marketing motions. Use Your Own Product

: In emerging markets, ecosystem advancement can benefit all players. The traditional SaaS sales playbook assumed predictable growth, high gross margins, and demand generation challenges. AI companies operate in a world of unpredictable hypergrowth, real marginal costs, and demand fulfillment opportunities. The companies that recognize this shift earliest—and adapt their go-to-market strategies accordingly—will define the next era of enterprise software.

:

:

Talia Goldberg (Bessemer)

Human-in-the-loop and AI orchestration are the most misunderstood concepts in B2B SaaS. 1️⃣ Most think "human-in-the-loop" means AI makes their work easier. Wrong. 👋 It means humans handle the cases AI can't solve. All day long. In real time, or as close as possible. The 30% of support tickets that are too complex. The sales conversations that need real judgment. The edge cases that break automated systems. 🚵 As AI gets better, the remaining human work gets HARDER, not easier. 2️⃣ And "orchestration" isn't picking vendors and watching dashboards. It's 60+ days of intensive training after deployment. Daily quality auditing. Managing 5-10 AI systems that each have unique failure modes. 👉 SaaStr's reality check: We sent 4,495 AI emails with top response rates, but it required: • 90 minutes every morning training the AI • 1 hour every night reviewing performance • Real-time responses throughout the day • 20+ million words of training content 🫵 Doing AI right is more work than not using AI at all Perplexity's CBO revealed another layer at SaaStr AI Summit 2025: AI changes WHEN you work, not just what you do. Sales reps now use AI live during prospect calls, making split-second decisions about what intelligence to surface while maintaining authentic conversations. Support already proved this model works: • Decagon: 70% deflection rates • Duolingo: 80%+ automation • Intercom: 86% resolution rates But those numbers hide the human orchestration behind them. Support teams evolved into AI managers, not disappearing but becoming more specialized. They do the tough stuff now. The multiplication effect hits when you deploy >multiple< AI systems. Now you need people who understand how your chatbot's limitations interact with your email automation's strengths. How to prevent AI systems from amplifying each other's errors.
